# Blinkered 



- The tightening in some time spreads and firming in physical premiums that have accompanied the sharp decline in base metals prices reflect the continued improvement in the fundamental picture. It is ironic that the market’s attention has shifted away from physical indicators just when they are looking the strongest they have been in some time. In particular, demand concerns for some metals seem excessive, with global aluminium demand running at record high, and copper and nickel demand only marginally below their historical peaks. 

- In our view, China has hit a pivot point. With copper supply chain inventory fully destocked, participants are now drawing on SHFE and bonded stocks. Even scrap is tighter. As our focus section analyses, we believe scrap usage is being maximised and do not believe it will offer a reprieve from a supply-constrained market.

For the same reason, we have also lowered our price expectations for the other base metals, apart from aluminium. Given booming and broad-based global demand, we now see price strength continuing through H2 and have raised our forecast higher to reflect this. 

- Precious metals prices have come under pressure as the dollar has strengthened, concerns over a slowdown have materialised, and successive increases in margin requirements have weighed upon silver. #### **FOCUS: UNTANGLING THE SCRAP DIMENSION TO BASE METALS IN 2011** 

## **Scrapping our way to the truth** 

- _The scrap market is a significant component in fundamental dynamics for base metals. In this focus piece, we consider the effect of scrap market fundamentals on the copper and aluminium markets in 2011 and beyond._ 

- _Given mine supply tightness, scrap will be key for growth in refined copper output this year. We believe that the strong price signal, growing industrial activity and continued improvement in emerging market scrap supply chains will lead to further growth in global scrap supply this year._ 

- _But the degree of copper scrap supply improvement will be constrained by limitations on old scrap supply, with little latent material to use. We believe that scrap usage is already being maximised through the copper supply chain, but do not believe that this will offer a sudden reprieve from a supply-constrained market._ 

- _In a tight primary aluminium market, exacerbated by financing deals, scrap demand has risen. However, beyond short-term factors such as the effect of the Japan earthquake on autos, we see no reason to believe that scrap supply should improve enough in 2011 to plug the gap. The key remains an increase in obsolete scrap supply in China to a level of equilibrium with demand growth from semis, and that remains some years off, with the scrap market remaining tight in the interim._ 

A search on Metal Bulletin reveals more than 50 stories this year alone about metal thefts, the BBC has also reported a number of stories on the topic and just last week, Reuters reported that British Railways cable thefts had jumped 67% this year. The increased occurrences of metal thefts illustrate the high value being placed on scrap metal and the strong demand for it. Scrap forms an important part of the copper and aluminium markets, yet it is all too often overlooked, mainly because it is an incredibly opaque industry about which is very difficult to obtain information. Nevertheless, the ebb and flow of scrap availability has important implications for the refined copper and primary aluminium markets, accounting for more than a third of the copper industry and more than a quarter of the aluminium industry. In this month’s focus, we analyse the methods by which scrap penetrates the copper and aluminium markets, changes in scrap usage trends and the outlook for scrap supply and its implications for refined and primary metals markets. 

###### **Scrap plays a volatile role in the copper market** 

_Scrap accounts for a third of the copper

market_ 

In the copper market, scrap enters the system through two routes: production (through its use in the refining process) and consumption (through its use in semi-fabricated products). This means that scrap can be a competitor with concentrate (in the production process) and refined metal (through consumption). 

_Scrap use is most flexible in copper refined output, less so in semis production_ 

Scrap use in refined output is more fluid and volatile than in consumption (semis) because there is more flexibility in the production process of the former. The amount of scrap that can be used in the production of refined copper is, in theory, almost limitless, bound only by availability and/or the technology in use. It is for this reason that there is such a big difference in the proportion of secondary in refined between countries. In Germany, for instance, the ratio is as high as almost 60%, while in the US it is 3% because the gradual decline in the manufacturing base and cheaper scrap processing costs in China have resulted in a large portion of US scrap now being exported for processing elsewhere. large manufacturing base of Germany generates a large volume of scrap, so the domestic industry has been structured to maximise this through having dedicated secondary smelters and through refineries having the technological capability to use large volumes of scrap. Illustrating the flexibility in this area of scrap use is the change in proportion of secondary used in refined output over the past two decades. This figure rose from just over 14% in the mid-1980s to almost 18% by the mid-1990s, falling to a low of 12% in 2003 before rising to a record high of over 19% in late 2010. The two key factors behind the changes in scrap use in refined output are supply and price, which we will discuss in the next section. 

_Secondary in refined copper output is becoming an increasingly important source of supply_ 

Over the past decade, the trend has been a steady increase in the proportion of secondary used in refined output. Indeed, it has been the stronger growth in both secondary refined output and SXEW cathode production that has been responsible for much of the growth in refined output in recent years, with primary copper output constrained by tight concentrate availability. Although SXEW cathode output and secondary refined output are still far smaller contributors to total refined output (accounting for about 35%) than primary (which accounts for 65%). The single most important factor behind the increase in global secondary refined output is increase industrial activity resulting in a steady increase in scrap generation. The source of this has predominantly been the industrialisation of the emerging markets, in particular China. Chinese secondary refined output has grown 17% over the past decade, while for the world ex-China, this has actually declined slightly. This is largely a fu

nction of the flow of scrap into China, with the explosion of low-cost Chinese secondary facilities attracting large import volumes of historically low copper content scrap. Indeed, outside China, secondary as a share of refined has actually fallen from 13% to 11%, while in China it has risen from 26% to 38% over the past decade. The jump in Chinese scrap imports has played a key role in raising its share of secondary refined output, though increased domestic scrap generation has played a part. The supply of “old” life cycle scrap is largely a function of price, whilst the supply of “new” clean post-consumer scrap is largely a function of industrial activity. In secondary refined production, the use of scrap is directly a function of availability. This is because in secondary refined output, there are lower metallurgical barriers and in theory an almost limitless amount of scrap that can be used, which is not the case in semis production. So the more scrap there is around, the more scrap will be used in secondary refined output. When industrial output is strong, and scrap generation is therefore high, more scrap is typically used in refine

d output, while in periods of recession, low manufacturing and lower prices, there is less secondary in refined production. _The supply of “old” scrap will always be constrained by the level of past consumption_ However, there is also an indirect relationship with price. That is because the availability of this scrap will depend on the level of industrial activity (cars being scrapped and old buildings being torn down) and price. When prices are rising, it creates more of an incentive to recover old scrap, so an environment of rising or high prices will encourage more old scrap into the system. Indeed, this has been the pattern for some years, as rising copper prices have squeezed most of the latent scrap out of the system. This source of scrap supply is tied to the life cycle of goods and therefore the volume of old scrap that can be tapped into, for any given price, is constrained by the level of consumption in the past. For instance, the amount of automotive scrap available now will be largely determined by the size of the automotive market 15 years ago. Therefore, regardless of price, there are limitations on the potential growth in supply of old scrap. Exacerbating this is the trend over recent years of sustained high prices squeezing out all latent scrap from the system, leaving very little untapped sources of old scrap. ###### **How much could scrap use increase?** A conventional copper smelter will typically have a maximum scrap usage of 15-20%, although depending on the number of scrap smelters and the availability of scrap, this number can rise significantly. In Germany, where there is a large and established scrap processing industry and dedicated scrap smelters, the ratio of secondary refined production is as high as 60%. This illustrates how much propensity there is to raise scrap in refined output. But the major obstacle to growing this figure is the pace and scale of current growth relative to past consumption. For instance, scrap often has extra impurities that have negative environmental effects in burning. Handling it can also be difficult. Scrap can be difficult to load efficiently, raising the risk of disruptions or slowing down processing. Therefore, its use in semis is more than just a simple function of supply. It is also a function of price spreads. Because of quality issues, semi-fabricators will tend to prefer to use refined copper as opposed to scrap. However, in an environment where scrap discounts are wide, there is a bigger price incentive to maximise scrap usage. When discounts are small, fabricators will again increase the proportion of refined metal used in their raw material mix because the smaller discount is not enough to outweigh the added complexities of using more scrap. For instance, scrap introduces impurities into the furnace that would degrade the refractory and the brick lining. ###### **Scrap in the emerging markets** _A huge “scrap gap” exists in China_ There is often the misconception that recycling rates in China are low. In fact, the complete opposite is true. As with many emerging markets, the scarcity in raw materials in China has forced the country to be an extremely efficient recycler with very high recovery rates, especially given that lower labour and unit costs mean that even poor grades of scrap are processed. The block in the pipeline is in distribution networks. The small scale of the processors and the inefficient cross-provincial networks mean that the industry is often clunky and inefficient. However, the Chinese government is rapidly addressing this; in the 12th five-year plan, the government aims to consolidate the industry and make it more efficient by eliminating small scale recyclers. Even though China is an efficient recycler, it still has a huge “scrap gap” because of its early stage of economic development. This means that there is only a tiny pool of domestic life cycle scrap that it can tap. Consequently, it has become a large importer of scrap, with 65% of global imports going there. Large imports of old scrap have been key to assisting China’s growth in refined output, given its small domestic resource of mined copper relative to metal demand. These imports have played a big

role in raising China’s secondary refined production to 38% of total refined output from 26% a decade ago. Scrap imports have been encouraged by a favourable rebate system, whereby they used to obtain a 50% VAT rebate, the aim of which was to bring more regulation onto the industry to move it from the unofficial economy. However, the elimination of this rebate in January 2011 has effectively has raised the cost of scrap relative to cathode and could subsequently result in a sharp slowdown in scrap imports, particularly if discounts to cathodes narrow.

###### **Scrap supply in 2011 and beyond** 

_Scrap will not be a reprieve for copper’s tight supply conditions_ 

- In the copper market, where growth in raw material supply from mines continues to stagnate scrap supply and the ability to grow scrap supply is a key factor for the refined market balance and prices, we believe that copper mine output will be largely flat this year, indeed with the risk skewed to a potential decline. This means that the growth in refined output will have to come from scrap. Is this possible, given the already large rebound in scrap supply in 2010? Certainly, the incentive has never been as strong. The difficulty in sourcing concentrate and the poor outlook for mine supply, together with high prices, are creating an environment conducive to maximising scrap use throughout the entire market chain. We believe that the strong price signal, growing industrial activity and continued improvement in emerging market scrap supply chains will lead to further growth in global scrap supply this year and beyond, though the scale of the increase will be constrained. Old scrap supply is tied to the life cycle of goods, which means that the volume of old scrap that can be tapped into, for any given price, is constrained by the level of consumption in the past. Therefore, regardless of price, there are limitations on the potential growth in supply of old scrap. Certainly, as China continues to mature, the volume of old scrap that can be tapped will steadily, increase though we believe that the growth in current consumption will far outpace the growth in old scrap for some time yet. Incentive schemes such as Cash for Clunkers that encourage the trading in of old products, eg, autos and consumer goods, for discounts on new ones, do provide a temporary boost to old scrap supply, though only by bringing it forward. We believe that scrap usage is already being maximised through the copper supply chain, but given the limitations outlined above, we do not believe that this will offer a sudden reprieve from a supply constrained market. Indeed, in our forecast market balance we already forecast scrap growth usage in 2011 (for fabricators, smelter and refiners) of close to 20% y/y.

###### **Placing scrap in the aluminium market balance** _Given tightness in the spot primary market, can scrap supply offer a moderating effect?_ While the copper scrap picture has received heightened attention recently due to extreme raw material constraints, we believe the aluminium scrap market also requires close attention in 2011. The spot primary aluminium market has also begun this year in tight fashion. Following a negligible market surplus of 150Kt in 2010 (representing just 0.3% of global consumption), in the first quarter of 2011, the global market balance slipped into marginal deficit. Exacerbated by warehouse financing deals, primary spot physical market conditions have evolved in a direction of tightness. Physical premiums in Europe and the US Midwest have soared to multi-year highs, with reports of waiting times of over six months to withdraw material from some warehouses in the US. The question, therefore, is whether the aluminium scrap supply can potentially moderate the tightness in the spot primary market and, hence, premiums, or alternatively, offer another dimension of tightness in the overall aluminium market picture in 2011? - _Scrap unlikely to offer a bail out with spreads to remain tight_ In our view, the answer is in the negative. While higher LME aluminium prices and rising semis output (as a function of generally robust levels of industrial production) present a picture of r

ising post-industrial scrap supply, that in itself is likely to have a zero sum effect on scrap market balance, given this is driven by an equivalent increase in demand from semis for scrap as an input. Post-consumer (or obsolete scrap) supply remains a key variable. However, given there are no major scrap incentive programmes in the US or Europe this year (such as Cash for Clunkers in 2010) and in China current demand far exceeds growth in scrap from obsolescence goods, this is unlikely to offer an escape valve in 2011. The repercussions of the natural disaster in Japan via the auto sector may temporarily moderate demand for some forms of aluminium scrap, although the broader picture suggests a continued tight balance and essentially no bail-out for the spot primary market. 

###### **Aluminium scrap demand likely to rise** 

_Scrap represents over a quarter of overall global aluminium demand_ 

Given its opaque nature, quantifying the exact features of the scrap market remains a challenge. Broadly speaking, data suggest that over the past decade, scrap has represented 20-30% of total global aluminium consumption. Based on the somewhat crude differential between semis output (fabrication stage in the aluminium supply chain) and primary consumption, data imply that in 2000, scrap usage made up close to 29% of total aluminium demand, although by 2010 that figure had moderated to closer to 25% due to

disproportionately faster growth in Chinese demand diluting the overall figure. Such a figure does, however, conceal significant regional variations that are important to appreciate. Using the same methodology, over the past decade scrap usage as a proportion of total demand has averaged 33% in the US, 41% in Germany, 45% in Japan and perhaps most significantly only 18% in China (although this masks a rise from just 10% in 2000 to 26% in 2010). The key point, hence, is that scrap represents close to a quarter of the aluminium market and, thus, offers potentially significant fundamental influence. 

- _Scrap use depends on_ 

- _the type of semis product_ 

   - To examine the market dynamics for 2011 closer, it is important to have some understanding of the structure of the scrap market, linkage to the primary market and longer-term trends in usage and generation. Scrap demand of the proportion quoted is generated from semis producers, which can be characterised as fabricators producing foundry (diecasters), sheet (rolling mills) and extrusions (extruders), sourcing either primary aluminium or scrap to create their products. Scrap is sourced by either remelters or secondary smelters, who produce casthouse aluminium products that, to an extent, compete with alloy ingot produced by primary smelters. Due to the alloyed nature of scrap, remelters and secondary smelters produce only alloys. The degree to which these compete with primary aluminium depends largely on the type of fabricators product

. Diecasting is a form of semis production predominantly based on scrap, making up close to 95% of total aluminium used by the sector, and this is the case in both the West and China. In terms of milling and extrusions, the picture of scrap use is far more constrained, with the West and Brazil using 35-75% of scrap in some applications of extruders. In China, this figure falls to closer to 20%. - _There is certainly flex in some product areas to use higher scrap input_ - There is certainly flex in the system to use higher amounts of scrap, undoubtedly so in China, but also in the West in some product areas. In the can sheet/packaging sector, body sheets are already pushing 90% scrap usage, so feasibly cannot go any higher. However, while extrusions use on average 40% of scrap, some producers have recently trialed an extruded billet out of 100% scrap for green building certification, but the market remains embryonic. There are limiting factors in some product areas, due to the finishing characteristics, where too high a proportion of scrap means it is difficult to anodize or results in a different appearance to virgin aluminium. Source: Brazilian Aluminium Association, Barclays Capital 16 May 2011 10 **Barclays Capital | Metals Magnifier** ###### **Obsolescence the key to future scrap supply** _Post-industrial scrap supply growth closely correlated to industrial demand_ _Transportation is a source of tightness for old scrap until new higher content vehicles reach the end of their life_ _Can recycling rates likely to rise, while electronics scrap supply will benefit from shorter lifecycle_ The supply picture of the aluminium scrap market can, as with copper, essentially be divided into two segments; new scrap generated during the initial manufacturing process (postindustrial), which is recycled in situ or sent to remelters/secondary smelters, or old scrap, which is collected after consumer use has run its course (post-consumer). In terms of a distribution between new and old scrap, global data are sparse, but in the US in 2010, the USGS reporte

d the ratio at 59:41, while the EAA reported that for Europe in 2008 at 63:32. In China, while no figures exist, new scrap is the overwhelming dominant source of supply, given the small pool of old scrap due to lower past consumption levels. From a post-industrial perspective, the recovery loop is essentially efficient, with no significant regional variations (including China), and is unlikely to offer any significant shift in influence on scrap supply in the near term. Volumes change with the levels of semis output, but given geographically consistent levels of efficiency (hence, little flex for improvement) and a direct correlation to rising demand from semis for scrap, it is not a key differentiating fundamental factor. 

Post-consumer scrap generation is, however, a far more significant variable supply influence on the scrap market balance. Old scrap comes from the key aluminium consuming endproduct sectors. A recent European Commission (EC) report stated that on a global scale, the breakdown of old scrap supply can be given as the transportation sector providing 44%, the packaging sector 28%, cable & wire combined with electronics 21%, and the construction and building sector 7%. The rate of reclamation within each sector depends largely on its scrap processing technology and societal commitment to the collection process. The transport sector is the largest supplier of old aluminium scrap and has a high reclamation rate, with EC data stating the end of life vehicle rate of collection is 85% in the US, Europe and Japan. Over the past decade, however, the transport sector has been a source of growing tightness for scrap, primarily due to two factors. First, the rising level of aluminium in vehicles has offered an increasing source of demand. For example, in the 1990s, the average North American vehicle contained 75Kg of aluminium, versus 150Kg in 2009. Second, given that the average lifetime of vehicles is 12-15 years, the higher aluminium content vehicles will not start reaching the end of the life span until the mid2010s at the earliest; hence, in the meantime, it provides a deficit drag on the system. Incentive programmes such as Cash for Clunkers in the US may encourage early end of life decision-making, but such policies are not a feature of the market in 2011. 

- The sectors where potential old scrap supply is most likely to improve in the medium term are packaging and electronics. In the former (which provides 28% of old scrap), recycling rates vary considerably across the globe, with the average rate of 36% masking performance from as low as 25% to as high as 85%. These variations are most visible in the used beverage can sector, where some nations such as Brazil (97%) and Japan (91%) achieve far higher collection rates than other regions such as the US (54%) and Europe (63%). Higher rates are largely achieved as a function of the incentive and accessibility mechanisms of the collection process. Given there is growing emphasis on gree

ner policies by both US and European governments, it is likely that over time the laggards will improve rates and, hence, boost supply from this source. The electronics sector is also likely to offer an improved source of scrap. ###### **China the key to future supply improvement** 

- _China lags the West in scale of scrap usage and supply_ 

Ultimately, though, the key question with regards to old scrap supply is more geographical that sectoral. As the world’s largest producer and consumer of aluminium, China is the crucial fundamental factor in the primary aluminium balance. Its scrap sector is very much a laggard in comparison. Indeed, broadly speaking, it is close to 20 years behind the West in terms of usage in the sheet mill and extrusions sectors, with only diecasting operating at a similar level of input. Overall scrap use registered at close to 26% in 2010, which offers a steady improvement from just 10% a decade earlier but still lags the rest of the world. It is, however, the supply side that is most critical, given that in China old scrap generation has barely to register as a supply variable. 

- _The short life of the majority of goods_ 

- _in China limits the degree of obsolescence_ 

So far in China, the pace of obsolete scrap generation has been low; hence, the dependence on primary supply has remained well established. In some respects, this is confusing, given the size of the Chinese economy and robust levels of growth witnessed over the past decade – surely scrap should be plentiful? However, it is the recent nature of this growth story which means that old scrap generation has been constrained. Essentially, there is very little old ‘stuff’ in China. Sectors such as autos or electronic appliances have increased their output levels at an exponential rate over the past few years. For example, motor vehicle production has increased from 1.8mn units in 1999 to close to 14mn units in 2009, while air conditioners have increased from 13mn units to 81mn units over the same period. The point is that China has yet to reach the stage where old scrap generation has reached anywhere near an equilibrium with demand for goods containing aluminium. This situation is unlikely to change over the next 5-10 years until cars/appliances start coming out of service, having originated from the sharp pickup in output in the 2000s. In the mean time, with obsolescence remaining low, the consu

mption of primary will have to remain high. That is not to say there is not the will in China to change the significance of the scrap sector – as with copper, the latest 12th Five-Year plan placed greater emphasis on recycling with the likely introduction of more recycling plants, which should spur greater usage, but this will take time to have a significant effect. ###### **Scrap supply in 2011 and beyond** The picture presented for the aluminium scrap market is one in which the critical variable in the global market dynamics is old scrap generation, and explicitly in China.
